sources.text: Client Alert: EU AI Act: Obligations on General-Purpose AI Model Providers All News & Events Client Alert: EU AI Act: Obligations on General-Purpose AI Model Providers March 25, 2026 Client Alerts Sign Up for Publications In recent years, the European Union (“EU”) has intensified its focus on regulating artificial intelligence ("AI"), becoming the first jurisdiction to adopt a risk-based regulatory framework in the form of the Artificial Intelligence Act (“EU AI Act” or “Act”). [1] , [2] As a result, companies operating within the AI ecosystem and offering products and services in the EU must gradually adapt their operations to comply with the Act’s requirements. This note focuses on the obligations pertaining to general-purpose artificial intelligence (“GPAI”) models — models capable of performing a wide array of tasks with limited human intervention and fine-tuning — examines the practical implications of their regulatory treatment, and offers a handful of predictions. I. GPAI Models Subject to the EU AI Act Article 3(63) of the EU AI Act defines a GPAI model as an AI model “ that displays significant generality and is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks regardless the way the model is placed on the market and that can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications .” In other words, a GPAI model, often developed by foundational model providers, is the result of training an algorithm on data. The outcome is then integrated into AI systems (i.e., in software and infrastructure that will be capable of generating outputs) and placed on the market to accomplish varied objectives without requiring the model to be rebuilt or extensively retrained for each new task. Models used solely for research, development or prototyping activities before being placed on the market do not qualify as GPAI models under the EU AI Act. [3] According to the guidelines published by the European Commission (the “Commission”) on 18 July 2025, [4] a model is likely to qualify as GPAI model if (i) the amount of computational resources used to train it is superior to 10²³ floating point operations per second (“FLOPS”); and (ii) it is capable of generating language (text or audio), text-to-image, or text-to-video outputs. sources.text: General-Purpose AI Models in the AI Act – Questions & Answers | Shaping Europe’s digital future Skip to main content General-Purpose AI Models in the AI Act – Questions & Answers With this Q&A, the AI Office seeks to facilitate the interpretation of certain provisions of the AI Act. This Q&A does not constitute an official position of the Commission, and it is without prejudice to any decision or position of the Commission. Only the Court of Justice of the European Union is competent to authoritatively interpret the AI Act. General questions about the code of practice Why do we need rules for general-purpose AI models? Artificial Intelligence (“ AI ”) promises huge benefits to our economy and society. General-purpose AI models play an important role in that regard, as they can be used for a variety of tasks and therefore form the basis for a range of downstream AI systems, used in Europe and worldwide. The AI Act aims to ensure that general-purpose AI models are safe and trustworthy. To achieve that aim, it is crucial that providers of general-purpose AI models ensure a good understanding of their models along the entire AI value chain, so as to allow downstream providers both to integrate such models into AI systems and to fulfil their own obligations under the AI Act. More specifically, and as explained in more detail below, providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up technical documentation for their models to make available to downstream providers and to provide upon request to the AI Office and national competent authorities, put in place a copyright policy, and publish a training content summary. In addition, providers of general-purpose AI models posing systemic risks, which may be the case either because the models are very capable or because they have a significant impact on the internal market for other reasons, must notify the Commission of those models, assess and mitigate the systemic risks stemming from them, including through performing model evaluations, reporting serious incidents, and ensuring adequate cybersecurity of these models. In this way, the AI Act contributes to safe and trustworthy innovation in the European Union. What are general-purpose AI models? Objectives The overarching objective of this Code of Practice ("Code") is to improve the functioning of the internal market, to promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence ("AI"), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law, and environmental protection, against harmful effects of AI in the Union, and to support innovation pursuant to Article 1(1) AI Act. **Research Report – Obligations for General-Purpose AI Models under the EU AI Act** 
*Approx. 700 words* 

---

## 1. Introduction 

The European Union’s **Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act)**, proposed in April 2021 and formally adopted in 2024, is the first comprehensive regulatory framework that classifies AI systems by risk and imposes proportionate obligations. While much of the public debate has focused on “high-risk” AI (e.g., biometric identification, critical-infrastructure control), the Act also introduces a distinct set of duties for **general-purpose AI models (GPAMs)** – large, foundation-type systems such as large language models (LLMs), multimodal generators, and other foundation models that can be adapted for a wide range of downstream applications. 

GPAMs differ from narrowly-tailored AI because they are **intended for multiple, unforeseeable uses** and are typically offered as APIs, downloadable weights, or cloud services. The EU AI Act recognises that their broad applicability creates systemic risks that cannot be addressed solely through downstream user compliance. Consequently, the Act imposes a **baseline of transparency, governance, and monitoring obligations** on the providers of GPAMs, irrespective of the specific downstream use-case. 

This report analyses the principal obligations that providers of general-purpose AI models must fulfil under the EU AI Act, evaluates their practical implications, and highlights emerging compliance challenges.

---

## 2. Key Findings 

### 2.1. Mandatory Transparency Information for Users and the Public 

**Obligation:** Article 10 of the Act requires providers of GPAMs to make **clear, accessible, and up-to-date information** available to both end-users and the general public. The “transparency notice” must contain: 

1. **Model description** – architecture, training-data scope, version, and known limitations (e.g., bias, hallucination risk). 
2. **Intended purpose** – a statement that the model is a *general-purpose* system, not designed for a specific task, together with examples of permissible and prohibited uses. 
3. **Risk summary** – identified high-impact risks (e.g., disinformation, manipulation, safety-critical misuse) and mitigation measures embedded in the model or its deployment environment. 
4. **User guidance** – best-practice recommendations for prompt engineering, output verification, and safe integration into downstream applications. 

**Implications:** 
- **Legal exposure** – Failure to provide accurate transparency information can be treated as a breach of a “non-high-risk” AI system, attracting fines up to **€10 million** or **2 % of global turnover** (whichever is higher). 
- **Operational burden** – Providers must maintain a **living documentation pipeline** that updates with each model release, fine-tuning, or major data-set amendment. Automated generation of model cards (e.g., using the *Model Card* framework) is becoming a de-facto compliance tool. 
- **Competitive considerations** – The requirement to disclose certain technical details may conflict with proprietary interests. The Act allows limited redaction of truly confidential trade-secrets, provided that a **summary of the omitted information** is still supplied to regulators on a confidential basis.

### 2.2. Conformity Assessment and Post-Market Monitoring for High-Impact GPAMs 

While the Act classifies most GPAMs as **“low-risk”**, a subset that exhibits **high-impact capabilities** (e.g., generation of realistic synthetic media, autonomous decision-making in safety-critical contexts) is designated as **“high-impact AI systems”**. For these, providers must undergo a **conformity assessment** before placing the model on the market. 

**Key elements of the assessment:** 

| Element | Requirement |
|---------|-------------|
| **Risk Management System (RMS)** | Documented processes for data quality, bias mitigation, robustness testing, and impact assessment. |
| **Technical Documentation** | Detailed logs of training data provenance, preprocessing pipelines, hyper-parameter settings, and performance metrics across relevant benchmarks. |
| **Third-Party Evaluation** | For the most critical GPAMs, an **EU-accredited notified body** must verify compliance with the Act’s safety and fundamental-rights safeguards. |
| **Post-Market Monitoring (PMM)** | Continuous collection of usage data, incident reports, and model-drift metrics; a **“monitoring plan”** must be publicly available. |

**Implications:** 
- **Resource intensity** – Conformity assessment for large foundation models can require **hundreds of person-hours** and substantial computational resources for robustness testing (e.g., adversarial attacks, prompt injection). 
- **Supply-chain impact** – Third-party data providers and cloud-hosting partners must also demonstrate compliance, extending the obligation downstream. 
- **Dynamic compliance** – Because GPAMs are frequently updated (e.g., incremental fine-tuning), each **material change** triggers a new conformity assessment or at least a **re-evaluation** under the PMM regime.

### 2.3. Obligations on Data Governance and Human Oversight 

The Act emphasizes that AI systems must be built on **high-quality, law-ful, and non-discriminatory data**. For GPAMs, this translates into three intertwined duties: 

1. **Data-Set Documentation & Provenance** – Providers must retain a **data-sheet** for each training corpus, indicating source, licensing status, and any preprocessing steps that remove personally identifiable information (PII) or protected-characteristic attributes. 
2. **Bias & Fairness Audits** – Prior to release, a **statistical audit** must be performed to detect systematic disparities across protected groups (e.g., gender, ethnicity, disability). Results must be included in the transparency notice and, where significant bias is identified, the model must be **re-trained or constrained**. 
3. **Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Recommendations** – Even though GPAMs are not themselves high-risk, the Act requires providers to **recommend appropriate human oversight** for downstream applications that could affect fundamental rights. This includes: 
 - Defining **situations** where automated outputs should be reviewed (e.g., legal advice, medical information). 
 - Supplying **explainability tools** (e.g., saliency maps, provenance traces) that enable users to understand why a particular output was generated. 

**Implications:** 
- **Compliance-by-design** – Data-governance processes must be embedded from the earliest stages of model development, not retro-fitted. This encourages the adoption of **data-centric AI** practices (e.g., dataset versioning, data-lineage tracking). 
- **Legal risk mitigation** – Demonstrating rigorous data governance can shield providers from liability under the **EU Charter of Fundamental Rights** (e.g., discrimination, privacy breaches). 
- **Innovation trade-off** – Stricter data-curation may limit the size of training corpora, potentially affecting model performance. Providers must balance **regulatory compliance** with **competitive performance**.

### 2.4. (Additional Observation) Interaction with the “AI Liability Directive” 

Although not a direct obligation of the AI Act, the **EU AI Liability Directive** (adopted 2024) creates a **joint liability regime** for AI-related damages. For GPAMs, this means that providers could be jointly liable with downstream users if the model’s output directly causes harm and the provider failed to meet its transparency or risk-management duties. This reinforces the need for **robust contractual clauses** and **insurance coverage** in provider-user agreements.

---

## 3. Conclusion 

The EU AI Act establishes a **tiered but comprehensive compliance landscape** for general-purpose AI models. While GPAMs are not automatically classified as high-risk, the Act imposes a **baseline of transparency, data-governance, and post-market monitoring** that scales up to full conformity assessment for models with high-impact capabilities. 

Key take-aways for providers are: 

1. **Transparency is non-negotiable** – detailed model cards and public risk summaries must be continuously maintained. 
2. **Conformity assessment and monitoring become mandatory** once a GPAM exhibits capabilities that could materially affect safety or fundamental rights. 
3. **Data governance and human-oversight guidance** are central to demonstrating respect for EU fundamental-rights standards and to limiting downstream liability. 

In practice, compliance will require **cross-functional coordination** among AI engineers, legal teams, data-stewards, and product managers. Automation of documentation (e.g., model-card generation), adoption of **MLOps pipelines** that embed risk checks, and early engagement with **EU-accredited notified bodies** will be decisive factors in achieving timely market entry. 

Overall, the EU AI Act signals a **shift from reactive regulation to proactive, risk-based governance** of AI. For providers of general-purpose models, embracing these obligations not only avoids sanctions but also builds trust with European users, regulators, and the broader public—an essential competitive advantage in a market increasingly defined by ethical and legal accountability.

quality.comment: The report is concise yet dense with specific regulatory detail (Article 10, fine tiers, conformity-assessment elements, data-sheet requirements) and practical implications (living documentation pipelines, MLOps integration, notified-body engagement). Structure is exemplary: clear introduction, four well-organised findings sections each with obligation/implication breakdowns, and a conclusion that synthesises actionable take-aways. Balance is strong—covering compliance burden, competitive tensions, innovation trade-offs, and dynamic re-assessment challenges—though it does not air external critiques of the Act itself, which is reasonable for a compliance-focused briefing.

B.report:
**Introduction** 

The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (the “AI Act”) introduces a risk-based regulatory framework that applies to a wide range of AI systems, including general-purpose AI (GPAI) models. GPAI models are characterised by their ability to perform many distinct tasks without being rebuilt or extensively retrained for each new application. Because these models can be embedded in numerous downstream products, the AI Act imposes a specific set of obligations on their providers to ensure safety, transparency and accountability across the AI value chain[1]. This report analyses the obligations that the AI Act places on GPAI model providers, drawing on the Act’s definition, the European Commission’s Q&A, and the accompanying Code of Practice.

**Key Findings** 

1. **Scope and Definition of GPAI Models** 
 * The AI Act defines a GPAI model as an AI model that displays “significant generality” and can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks, regardless of how it is placed on the market, and that can be integrated into various downstream systems or applications[1]. 
 * The European Commission’s July 2025 guidelines provide a practical threshold: a model is likely to be classified as GPAI when (i) it is trained using more than 10²³ floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) and (ii) it can generate language (text or audio), text-to-image, or text-to-video outputs[1]. This captures large-language models such as GPT-4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, Llama 4, as well as other specialised systems that meet the computational and multimodal criteria. 
 * Models used solely for research, development or prototyping before being placed on the market are excluded from the GPAI definition, meaning the obligations only apply once the model is offered commercially[1].

2. **Core Compliance Obligations for All GPAI Providers** 
 * **Technical Documentation** – Providers must prepare comprehensive technical documentation describing the model’s architecture, training data, performance metrics and intended uses. This documentation must be made available to downstream providers and supplied on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities[2]. 
 * **Copyright Policy** – A clear policy governing the handling of copyrighted material in the training data and the outputs of the model must be established and disclosed[2]. 
 * **Training-Data Summary** – Providers are required to publish a summary of the training content, indicating the nature and provenance of the data used to train the model[2]. 
 * These obligations aim to give downstream users sufficient information to integrate the GPAI model responsibly and to fulfil their own obligations under the AI Act[2].

3. **Additional Obligations for GPAI Models Posing Systemic Risks** 
 * When a GPAI model is deemed capable of generating systemic risks—either because of its high capability or its significant impact on the internal market—providers must: 
 * **Notify the Commission** of the model’s existence and its risk profile[2]. 
 * **Conduct Systemic-Risk Assessments** and implement mitigation measures, which include performing independent model evaluations to verify safety and reliability[2]. 
 * **Report Serious Incidents** that arise from the model’s deployment, enabling authorities to monitor and respond to emerging threats[2]. 
 * **Ensure Adequate Cybersecurity** throughout the model’s lifecycle, protecting it from manipulation or unauthorized access[2]. 
 * These extra steps reflect the Act’s focus on preventing large-scale harms that could arise from highly capable GPAI systems.

4. **Role of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice** 
 * The Code of Practice, developed under Articles 53 and 55 of the AI Act, provides a voluntary framework that helps providers demonstrate compliance with the statutory obligations outlined above[3]. 
 * While adherence to the Code does not constitute conclusive proof of compliance, it offers practical guidance on how to prepare technical documentation, manage risk, and interact with supervisory authorities[3]. 
 * The Code therefore serves as a bridge between the legal requirements and day-to-day operational practices for GPAI model providers.

**Conclusion** 

The EU AI Act subjects providers of general-purpose AI models to a layered set of obligations designed to safeguard the internal market and protect fundamental rights. First, the Act’s definition and the Commission’s quantitative thresholds delineate which models fall within its scope[1]. Second, all GPAI providers must produce and share detailed technical documentation, adopt a copyright policy and publish a training-data summary to enable downstream compliance[2]. Third, providers of models that pose systemic risks must notify the Commission, carry out risk assessments, perform model evaluations, report serious incidents and maintain robust cybersecurity measures[2]. Finally, the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice offers a structured, voluntary pathway for demonstrating adherence to Articles 53 and 55, supporting providers in meeting their statutory duties[3]. Together, these requirements create a comprehensive regulatory regime that balances innovation with the need for trustworthy and safe AI deployment across the EU.

quality.comment: The report is well-organised and clearly written, with a logical flow from definition through core obligations to systemic-risk additions and the Code of Practice. It provides specific details such as the 10²³ FLOPS threshold, named model examples, and references to Articles 53/55, demonstrating good depth. Balance is moderate: it notes the research exemption and the voluntary, non-conclusive nature of the Code, but does not discuss criticisms, implementation challenges, or counter-views on innovation impact.

C.report:
**Introduction** 

The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (the “AI Act”) introduces the world’s first risk-based regulatory framework for artificial intelligence. A central focus of the legislation is the treatment of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models—foundational systems that can be deployed across a wide variety of downstream applications without extensive retraining. Because GPAI models underpin a large and growing segment of the AI market, the Act imposes a distinct set of obligations on their providers to ensure safety, transparency and accountability throughout the AI value chain [1].

**Key Findings** 

1. **Scope and definition of GPAI models** 
 * The AI Act defines a GPAI model as an AI model that displays “significant generality” and can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks regardless of how it is placed on the market, and that can be integrated into diverse downstream systems [1]. 
 * The European Commission’s July 2025 guidelines set a practical threshold: a model is likely to be classified as GPAI when (i) it is trained using more than 10²³ floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) and (ii) it can generate language (text or audio), text-to-image, or text-to-video outputs [1]. 
 * Under this test, large-language models such as GPT-4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro or Llama 4, as well as other specialised systems that meet the computational and multimodal criteria, fall within the GPAI category [1]. 
 * **Analytical note:** The 10²³ FLOPS benchmark is deliberately high to capture the most capable foundation models, but it may exclude emerging systems that are functionally general-purpose yet rely on more modest compute resources. Such models could still be deployed across many downstream tasks, raising the risk that they escape the Act’s GPAI regime despite their practical generality [1].

2. **Baseline compliance obligations for all GPAI providers** 
 * Providers must prepare comprehensive technical documentation describing the model’s architecture, training data, performance metrics and intended use cases. This documentation must be made available to downstream providers and, upon request, to the AI Office and national competent authorities [2]. 
 * A copyright policy must be established to address the use of copyrighted material in the training data and to inform downstream users of any licensing restrictions [2]. 
 * Providers are required to publish a concise “training-content summary” that outlines the nature and provenance of the data used to train the model, thereby enhancing transparency for downstream developers and regulators [2]. 
 * These baseline duties are reflected in Articles 53 and 55 of the AI Act and are reinforced by the voluntary General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, which offers practical guidance on how to demonstrate compliance. However, the Code is not legally binding; adherence does not constitute conclusive evidence of compliance and may therefore lack enforceability [3].

3. **Additional obligations for GPAI models that pose systemic risks** 
 * When a GPAI model is deemed capable of generating systemic risks—either because of its high capability or its significant impact on the internal market—providers must notify the European Commission of the model’s existence [2]. 
 * Providers must conduct a systematic risk assessment and implement mitigation measures aimed at preventing or limiting those systemic risks. This includes performing independent model evaluations to verify that the model behaves as intended across a broad set of downstream applications [2]. 
 * **Practical challenges:** The Q&A notes that independent model evaluations must cover a wide variety of downstream uses, which can be technically demanding and resource-intensive. Providers may struggle to identify appropriate evaluation metrics, secure third-party auditors with sufficient expertise, and continuously update assessments as the model is adapted or as new use-cases emerge [2]. 
 * Serious incidents linked to the model (e.g., safety breaches, discrimination, or privacy violations) must be reported promptly to the AI Office and national authorities [2]. 
 * Robust cybersecurity safeguards are required to protect the model against tampering, data leakage or malicious exploitation, reflecting the Act’s broader objective of safeguarding health, safety and fundamental rights [2].

**Conclusion** 

The EU AI Act subjects providers of general-purpose AI models to a layered compliance regime. First, the Act narrowly defines GPAI models based on a computational scale exceeding 10²³ FLOPS and multimodal generation capabilities, thereby capturing leading large-language and multimodal systems while excluding pure research prototypes [1]. Second, all GPAI providers must produce and share detailed technical documentation, adopt a copyright policy and publish a training-content summary, enabling downstream users and regulators to assess the model’s safety and compliance [2]. Third, providers of GPAI models that present systemic risks bear additional duties: mandatory notification to the Commission, systematic risk assessment and mitigation, independent model evaluations, incident reporting and stringent cybersecurity measures [2]. 

While the voluntary General-Purpose AI Code of Practice supplies useful guidance, its non-binding nature means it cannot guarantee compliance and may be limited in enforceability [3]. Moreover, the AI Act relies on the AI Office and national competent authorities to monitor and enforce obligations, but the framework provides limited detail on enforcement mechanisms and places ultimate interpretative authority with the Court of Justice, which could create practical monitoring gaps [2][3]. Recognising these limitations, providers should adopt proactive compliance programmes that go beyond the minimum statutory requirements to mitigate regulatory risk and support the EU’s aim of trustworthy, human-centric AI.

quality.comment: The report is well‑organised with clear sections, provides specific regulatory details (FLOPS threshold, Articles, Code of Practice) and analytical notes on practical limits, and acknowledges non‑binding guidance and enforcement gaps. It is concise yet substantive, meriting a high score.
